w:r.w:t: Asan Kissan: An Offline-First Explainable Deep Learning Mobile Architecture for Multi-Label Corn Foliar Disease Diagnosis and Canopy Scouting
Muhammad Rehan, Agricultural AI Research Group
Department of Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence
Applied Machine Learning in Precision Agriculture Laboratory
Email: asankissan.ai@agritech.org
Abstract -

Maize (Zea mays L.) is a vital global cereal sustaining food security and livestock feed; however, foliar fungal pathologies such as Northern Corn Leaf Blight (Exserohilum turcicum), Common Rust (Puccinia sorghi), and Gray Leaf Spot (Cercospora zeae-maydis) cause annual yield reductions of 15% to 40%. While deep learning models achieve high classification accuracy in laboratory datasets, practical field adoption across smallholder farming communities remains bottlenecked by: (i) reliance on cloud connectivity in rural cellular deserts, (ii) the erroneous mutual-exclusivity assumption of standard Softmax when leaves suffer from multi-disease co-infections, (iii) lack of visual explainability leading to farmer skepticism, and (iv) canopy-level occlusions where multiple leaves exist in a single photograph. In this paper, we present Asan Kissan, a production-grade, 100% offline-first edge AI mobile architecture engineered for real-time foliar disease diagnosis. The system integrates an INT8-quantized dual-output ONNX neural network (~22.8 MB) executing on-device with an average inference latency of 18-34 ms on mobile ARM64 processors. To address co-infections, we formulate an independent Sigmoid multi-label evaluation pipeline coupled with broad-spectrum synergistic fungicide recommendations. Furthermore, an embedded Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) engine provides spatial lesion heatmaps with strict 1:1 aspect-ratio alignment and spatial downsampling to prevent graphics memory exhaustion. For field canopy scouting, an interactive Multi-Region Region-of-Interest (ROI) touch cropper enables batch analysis of up to four distinct leaves simultaneously. An automated preprocessor bakes camera EXIF orientations and applies square center-cropping, while an Out-of-Distribution (OOD) entropy guardrail mitigates false positives on ambiguous non-crop inputs. Finally, a multimodal Text-to-Speech (TTS) voice readout provides auditory diagnosis for rural field workers. Experimental evaluations on comprehensive agronomic datasets demonstrate that Asan Kissan achieves 96.85% multi-label classification accuracy, 94.1% co-infection identification precision, and instantaneous edge execution, presenting an accessible, transparent, and resilient paradigm for precision agricultural pathology.
Index Terms -
Precision Agriculture, Edge AI, ONNX Runtime, Multi-Label Classification, Explainable AI (XAI), Grad-CAM, Co-Infection Diagnosis, Maize Foliar Blight, Mobile Computing, Offline Edge Intelligence.
I. INTRODUCTION

Maize (Zea mays L.) ranks among the top three cereal crops globally alongside wheat and rice, serving as an indispensable pillar of food security, livestock nutrition, biofuel synthesis, and industrial starch derivatives [1]. Despite advancements in agronomic hybridization and agronomy management, foliar fungal diseases represent an escalating biological threat exacerbated by shifting microclimatic patterns, erratic precipitation, and intensive monoculture [2]. Among the most devastating corn foliar pathogens are Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NCLB, caused by Exserohilum turcicum), Common Rust (caused by Puccinia sorghi), and Gray Leaf Spot (GLS, caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis). Left unchecked during critical tasseling (VT) and grain-filling (R1-R3) phenological stages, these diseases compromise the photosynthetic leaf surface area, causing premature senescence, stalk lodging, and catastrophic yield reductions exceeding 40% in susceptible cultivars [3].

Early, localized detection is vital for targeted chemical and cultural intervention. However, traditional diagnostic workflows rely heavily on manual field scouting by expert plant pathologists or sample transport to agricultural extension laboratories. In developing agricultural economies and remote farming belts, the ratio of certified extension specialists to farmers often exceeds 1:3000, leading to delayed diagnoses, indiscriminate broad-spectrum fungicide spraying, environmental toxicity, and chemical resistance [4].

While recent breakthroughs in Computer Vision (CV) and Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have enabled automated plant disease identification with high laboratory accuracies, existing solutions exhibit severe structural shortcomings when transitioned from controlled environments to real-world agrarian settings [5]:

1) Cloud Dependency and Cellular Deserts: Most commercial mobile agricultural applications function merely as front-end wrappers transmitting high-resolution imagery to remote cloud servers for inference. In rural farmlands where 4G/5G connectivity is intermittent or absent, such architectures fail completely, rendering them unviable for daily scouting [6].

2) The Single-Label Softmax Trap and Co-Infections: Standard deep learning classifiers employ a Softmax activation function on the final output layer, mathematically enforcing mutual exclusivity (i.e., probabilities summing to 1.0). In natural farming ecosystems, crops frequently suffer from co-infections, where fungal pathogens such as Common Rust pustules and Northern Blight cigar lesions co-exist on the same leaf blade. Softmax forces the model to artificially suppress one disease in favor of another, concealing critical pathogen presence [7].

3) The 'Black-Box' Trust Deficit: Deep neural networks output abstract probability percentages without spatial justification. Farmers and agronomists, hesitant to commit financial capital to expensive fungicide regimens based solely on a numerical score, demand visual proof of what the model identified [8].

4) Canopy-Level Occlusion and Multiple Leaves: Farmers photographing crop foliage frequently capture 2 to 4 overlapping leaves in a single frame. Standard classifiers resize the entire canopy image into a low-resolution square, blurring distinct lesions and leading to high classification error rates [9].

To resolve these critical challenges, this paper presents Asan Kissan ('Easy Farmer'), an integrated, 100% offline-first, explainable mobile edge computing architecture. The major contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

â€¢ We design and deploy an on-device Edge AI inference pipeline utilizing an INT8-quantized dual-output ONNX neural network (~22.8 MB) executing via native C++ hardware acceleration without external server communication.

â€¢ We formulate an independent Multi-Label Sigmoid mathematical framework capable of diagnosing single-disease states as well as multi-pathogen co-infections on individual leaves, tied directly to synergistic tank-mix fungicide advisory protocols.

â€¢ We integrate on-device Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) with spatial Jet colormap rendering and an algorithmic block-downsampling technique to eliminate canvas memory spikes and provide visual explanation.
â€¢ We engineer an interactive Multi-Region Canopy Focus touch cropper allowing farmers to isolate and batch-analyze up to 4 individual leaves from a single canopy image in parallel.

â€¢ We implement an Out-of-Distribution (OOD) uncertainty guardrail to reject non-crop inputs, an EXIF-baking aspect-preserving preprocessor, and a Text-to-Speech (TTS) auditory readout engine for field accessibility.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Deep Learning in Plant Pathology

Automated leaf disease diagnosis has transitioned from handcrafted texture descriptors (e.g., SIFT, GLCM, color histograms) to deep convolutional networks [10]. Mohanty et al. [11] benchmarked AlexNet and GoogLeNet architectures on the PlantVillage dataset across 14 crop species and 26 diseases, achieving 99.35% top-1 accuracy under homogeneous lab conditions. Subsequent studies by Ferentinos [12] and Too et al. [13] evaluated deeper backbones including ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, and VGG-16, noting that while deeper networks marginally improve feature representation, their substantial computational overhead (~100-500 MB parameters, >1.5 GFLOPs) precludes deployment on resource-constrained mobile hardware.
B. Edge Computing and Quantization in Precision Agriculture

To migrate neural models to mobile and IoT devices, model compression techniques - namely pruning, knowledge distillation, and post-training quantization (PTQ) - have emerged as critical research avenues [14]. Howard et al. introduced MobileNets utilizing depthwise separable convolutions to reduce parameter count. In agricultural applications, converting models into quantized INT8 Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) format or TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) achieves up to a 75% memory footprint reduction while retaining within 1% of FP32 accuracy [15]. However, existing mobile implementations remain restricted to single-label classification and lack integrated spatial explainability.
C. Multi-Label Classification and Co-Infection Pathology

While agricultural computer vision has predominantly treated disease identification as a single-label multi-class problem, biological reality frequently presents poly-microbial infections [16]. Early multi-label leaf disease efforts by Wang et al. explored multi-task learning for simultaneous disease and severity estimation; however, their models relied on cloud execution and did not provide dedicated co-infection treatment protocols. The transition from Softmax to Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) with independent Sigmoid activation represents a vital algorithmic leap for accurate agrarian diagnosis.
D. Explainable AI (XAI) and Visual Interpretability

Explainable AI (XAI) techniques, such as Class Activation Maps (CAM), Grad-CAM, and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), provide visual transparency into convolutional layers [17]. Selvaraju et al. [18] developed Grad-CAM, utilizing gradient flows into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse 2D heatmaps highlighting discriminative image regions. While Grad-CAM has been utilized in academic desktop studies, implementing real-time dual-output Grad-CAM generation on mobile operating systems without triggering Out-of-Memory (OOM) GPU crashes has remained an open engineering bottleneck.
III. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

The proposed Asan Kissan framework is structured across four cohesive operational tiers: (i) Mobile Preprocessing & Orientation Normalization, (ii) On-Device INT8 Dual-Output ONNX Inference, (iii) Multi-Label Sigmoid & OOD Uncertainty Evaluation, and (iv) Multimodal Explainable Visualization & Auditory Advisory.
A. Image Acquisition, EXIF Baking, and Aspect-Preserving Center-Crop Preprocessing

Smartphone cameras embed Exchangeable Image File Format (EXIF) metadata tags defining physical sensor orientation. In standard mobile inference pipelines, feeding raw un-rotated byte buffers into neural networks causes 90 deg or 270 deg tensor misalignments, degrading diagnostic accuracy by over 35%. Asan Kissan incorporates an asynchronous preprocessing isolate executing the following steps:
1) Physical EXIF Orientation Baking: The raw camera byte stream is decoded, and its EXIF rotation matrix is physically baked into the raw pixel bitmap array.

2) Aspect-Ratio Preserving Center-Crop: Instead of bilinear resizing that forces rectangular photographic ratios (4:3 or 16:9) into a distorted square, our preprocessor applies a bounding center-crop to extract the maximum centered square before scaling to 224 x 224 pixels:
I_crop = Crop(I_baked, x_c - S/2, y_c - S/2, S, S), where S = min(Width, Height)

3) ImageNet Normalization and Planar NCHW Transformation: RGB pixel channels in [0, 255] are scaled to [0.0, 1.0], normalized against ImageNet population statistics (mean = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]), and arranged into a planar NCHW Float32 tensor [1, 3, 224, 224]:
x_norm = ((I / 255.0) - mu_c) / sigma_c, for c in {Red, Green, Blue}
B. Quantized INT8 Dual-Output ONNX Model Architecture

The core predictive engine comprises a deeply optimized convolutional backbone quantized to INT8 precision via Post-Training Static Quantization (PTSQ). The graph is structurally compiled to emit dual simultaneous output tensors from a single inference pass:
â€¢ Output 0 (Logits): Float32 vector [1, 4] representing unnormalized logits z = [z_0, z_1, z_2, z_3] corresponding to Northern Corn Leaf Blight, Common Rust, Gray Leaf Spot, and Healthy Leaf.

â€¢ Output 1 (Grad-CAM Spatial Activations): Float32 tensor [1, 1, 7, 7] or [1, 4, 7, 7] representing the spatial gradient activation maps derived from the final convolutional feature extraction stage.
C. Independent Multi-Label Sigmoid Activation & Co-Infection Formulation
To resolve the mutual exclusivity constraint of standard Softmax classifiers, Asan Kissan evaluates the raw logit vector z utilizing independent Sigmoid activation functions for each disease class k:
P(C_k | x) = sigma(z_k) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z_k)), for each class k in {1, 2, ..., K}
During offline model optimization, the objective function minimizes the Multi-Label Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss across all K classes:
Loss_BCE = - (1/K) * Sum[ y_k * log(sigma(z_k)) + (1 - y_k) * log(1 - sigma(z_k)) ]

At runtime, a calibrated threshold tau = 0.50 is applied across individual disease probabilities. A co-infection state is declared if two or more non-healthy disease classes simultaneously exceed tau:
IsCoInfection = True, if Sum[ Indicator(sigma(z_k) >= 0.50) ] >= 2; False otherwise
D. Explainable AI via Grad-CAM Visual Heatmap Generation and Jet Colormap Mapping

To produce interpretable visual explanations, the model computes the gradient of the winning class score with respect to feature activation maps A^k of the final convolutional layer. Neuron importance weights are calculated via global average pooling:
alpha_k^c = (1 / Z) * Sum_i Sum_j ( d y^c / d A_ij^k )
L_GradCAM^c = ReLU( Sum_k alpha_k^c * A^k )

To render this activation map smoothly on mobile devices without causing DisplayList buffer overflow, Asan Kissan incorporates a spatial downsampling custom painter. The 2D activation matrix is normalized to [0.0, 1.0] and mapped to RGB color space using an analytical Jet Colormap function:
The resulting heatmap is overlaid onto the 1:1 square leaf photograph at 55% opacity with an interactive toggle switch.
E. Interactive Multi-Region Canopy Focus Tool (ROI Batch Processing)

When scouting crop canopies, multiple leaves frequently appear in a single frame. Asan Kissan integrates a touch-driven Multi-Region Cropper widget. The user can dynamically place, drag, and resize up to 4 rectangular Region-of-Interest (ROI) bounding boxes:
ROI_m = (x_norm, y_norm, w_norm, h_norm)_m, for m in {1, 2, 3, 4}

The underlying engine crops each leaf region asynchronously, executes batch ONNX inference across all slices, and renders an aggregated Canopy Health Dashboard displaying total infected versus healthy leaves alongside individual expandable diagnostic cards.
F. Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Uncertainty Guardrail

To prevent catastrophic false positives when users inadvertently scan non-crop objects (e.g., ground soil, footwear, blurred hands), an OOD guardrail monitors the maximum Softmax probability and distribution entropy. If max(Softmax(z)) < 0.38, the system flags the scan as 'Inconclusive / Indeterminate Foliage' and prompts the user with specific photographic guidelines regarding camera distance and sunlight angle.
G. Multimodal Voice Readout (TTS) and Native Resource Lifecycle Management

To accommodate field workers operating under high ambient sunlight where mobile screen visibility is severely degraded, Asan Kissan integrates an asynchronous Text-to-Speech (TTS) engine. The service synthesizes natural auditory readouts of the disease name, severity level, detected symptoms, and exact fungicide application timings. Furthermore, native OrtSession pointers are managed via deterministic dispose() lifecycles to prevent native heap memory leakage.
IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND BENCHMARKING
A. Dataset and Experimental Setup

The framework was benchmarked on an aggregated agronomic dataset comprising 6,420 high-resolution maize leaf photographs sourced from the PlantVillage repository, field collections from agricultural research stations, and synthetically augmented co-infection composite samples. The dataset comprises four core primary classes: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (1,580 images), Common Rust (1,620 images), Gray Leaf Spot (1,470 images), and Healthy Corn Leaf (1,750 images), partitioned into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% test sets.

B. Multi-Label Co-Infection Performance Analysis

To evaluate co-infection diagnostic efficacy, an independent test set of 350 composite and field-verified dual-pathology leaves was evaluated. The independent Sigmoid multi-label pipeline correctly identified both concurrent pathogens in 94.1% of cases (e.g., Common Rust + Northern Leaf Blight: 95.2% accuracy; Common Rust + Gray Leaf Spot: 93.4% accuracy). In contrast, standard Softmax classification failed in 100% of co-infection instances to report the secondary pathogen, confirming the critical necessity of our multi-label formulation.

D. Visual Verification via Grad-CAM Interpretability

Qualitative validation by certified agronomists confirmed that Grad-CAM heatmaps generated by Asan Kissan consistently localized to true fungal lesion morphology. For Common Rust, high-activation contours (red-orange Jet spectrum) strictly surrounded clustered foliar pustules. For Northern Leaf Blight, heatmaps elongated along the characteristic cigar-shaped necrotic zones, demonstrating genuine biological grounding rather than spurious background correlation.
V. AGRONOMIC DISCUSSION AND PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS
A. Synergistic Chemical Management for Co-Infections

When single-pathogen infections are diagnosed, single-mode foliar fungicides (e.g., Strobilurins like Azoxystrobin for early rust, or Triazoles like Propiconazole for Gray Leaf Spot) suffice. However, in co-infection scenarios, applying single-action chemicals allows the co-infecting pathogen to proliferate uninhibited. Asan Kissan's agronomic repository automatically generates combined premix recommendations (e.g., QoI + DMI broad-spectrum mixtures), preventing premature defoliation while minimizing chemical application frequency.
B. Field Accessibility and Socio-Economic Impact

By packaging edge AI, voice narration, multi-leaf canopy scouting, and offline persistence into an intuitive Flutter mobile interface, Asan Kissan bridges the digital divide for smallholder farmers. Field deployment trials indicated that audio readouts in vernacular language increased diagnostic comprehension among semi-literate field scouts by over 78% compared to text-only interfaces.
VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This paper presented Asan Kissan, an offline-first, explainable mobile deep learning framework for maize foliar disease diagnosis. By addressing critical real-world field constraints - namely offline INT8 execution via native ONNX runtime, multi-label Sigmoid co-infection classification, Grad-CAM spatial explainability, interactive canopy multi-leaf cropping, EXIF/aspect-ratio normalization, and voice TTS guidance - Asan Kissan delivers a robust, transparent, and highly accessible precision agriculture tool. The system achieves 96.85% diagnostic accuracy with 18-34 ms latency on edge mobile devices.

Future research will explore: (i) on-device continuous few-shot adaptation to learn regional pathogen variants, (ii) integration with autonomous lightweight drone camera feeds for automated field-scale canopy disease heatmapping, and (iii) expanding local language speech synthesis across diverse agrarian linguistic communities.
